title: What the Net Cannot See
logline: Night after night, a small lagoon-fishing crew works by lamplight where most of what reaches them never becomes a catch, a flicker at the edge of sight, a sound not quite placed, and only a few signals ever become a decision to strike.
human_question: How much of what happens around us is ever actually noticed, and what decides which faint signal becomes an action?

premise.story: A lagoon or reef fishing crew works through a night shift by lamp and starlight, watching a float, listening for a splash, reading faint disturbances in dark water, most of which lead nowhere.
premise.place: A lagoon, estuary or shallow reef fished at night by lamplight.
premise.experience: The viewer sits inside long stretches of near-nothing broken by a handful of moments sharp enough to matter, and feels the gap between what merely touches the senses and what actually becomes an act.

concept_links.why: The source's six 'very slight object' processes describe contact so faint it barely disturbs the resting mind and produces no real knowing at all, 'seen, not seen; heard, not heard', which is close to a documentary truth about watching dark water for hours [C045-M:L20].
The source grades objects by how vivid they are, size, light, nearness, and how late they strike, which is exactly what separates a flicker a crew member ignores from the one they act on.
The eighteen rootless minds describe a layer of bare sensing that carries no verdict of its own; a fisher's glance at the water is this layer before any decision to strike is made.

what_camera_could_observe: Lamp sweeping dark water and the crew's eyes following it
A float or net line watched for long stretches with no visible change
A sudden turn of the head at a sound or ripple, followed by a decision to act or let it pass
Quiet talk between casts about what someone thought they saw
The catch, or the return with an empty net, at dawn
what_must_be_real: The crew's actual livelihood and risk; nothing staged for the camera, including any 'near miss' or dramatic strike. Participants describe what they noticed in their own words, not prompted by the interviewer.

possible_arc.opening: Lamp lit, boat pushed out, a long watch begins.
possible_arc.turn: A signal, a movement, a sound, is caught and acted on, or is let go.
possible_arc.ending_open: Dawn; the night's catch, whatever it is, and the crew's own account of what they noticed and missed.

position_hint: middle: an intimate, low-light film about the edge of perception, not an Object 5 acquisition scene.

requirements: A working lagoon, estuary or shallow reef fished at night
A crew willing to be filmed through long, low-light hours
Safe water access for a small camera crew at night

suggestions.name: Batticaloa Lagoon
suggestions.why: A well-known lagoon with an active night-fishing tradition.
suggestions.access_notes: Night filming on water requires careful safety planning.
suggestions.verify: Specific crews, access and current fishing patterns are unverified.

risks: Low light makes filming difficult and could tempt the crew to add light for the camera, changing the very conditions being observed
Dramatising a catch or a near-miss would be staging
Romanticising dangerous night work without showing its real economics
drop_if: No crew will allow a camera through an ordinary night shift without extra light or performance
The work cannot be filmed safely at night
Nothing distinguishes a noticed from an unnoticed signal in a way the camera can honestly show

connections.note: Both watch the line between a signal that barely registers and one that triggers a full response.

unknowns: No participant, access or event has been found or confirmed. Everything above is a research direction.
